description: AXIOON is a team focused on innovation, technology, and creative problem-solving. Our goal is to build useful solutions, share ideas, and bring them to life.
summary: Project AXIOON is a browser-based 3D game that turns space mission design into hands-on engineering. Players walk through a mission control center, pick a contract based on a real NASA mission (Artemis II, Mars 2020, OSIRIS-REx, DART and more), and build a multistage rocket from real engines. The game computes Δv with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation and thrust-to-weight ratio live, so every design choice has a visible physical consequence. Players then launch from an Orion-style cockpit, study their trajectory in a 3D orbit "X-ray" view, respond to in-flight anomalies drawn from real mission history, and receive a debrief that compares their flight with NASA's actual results. For the Space Mission Design challenge, our answer is to let players discover the physics by failing, reading a clear explanation of why, and trying again. It matters because orbital mechanics is usually taught through formulas alone. AXIOON runs in any modern browser with no installation, using open NASA/JPL data, making mission engineering accessible to students everywhere.
details:
Space Quest is an educational 3D game that takes the player through the full cycle of a real NASA mission: contract → rocket design → launch → flight → debrief. Our core design rule: the player discovers physics by making mistakes, not by reading about it.

HOW IT WORKS

1.⁠ ⁠Mission control hall. The player walks in third person through a 3D mission control center with a panoramic window onto the launch site, and uses three stations: the contract terminal, the holographic rocket builder and the launch console.

2.⁠ ⁠Real NASA missions. The contract board is a 3D Solar System with planets placed by JPL orbital elements. It offers seven missions: Artemis II (Moon), Mars 2020 Perseverance, OSIRIS-REx (Bennu), Psyche, Europa Clipper, Dragonfly (Titan) and DART (planetary defense). Each briefing separates real facts (dates, masses, results) from game parameters (budget, reward). A live radar shows current asteroid close approaches from NASA's NeoWs API.

3.⁠ ⁠Rocket engineering. The player assembles up to three stages from real engines (Merlin 1D, Merlin Vacuum, RS-25, RL10B-2), choosing engine count and propellant mass. The Tsiolkovsky equation Δv = Isp · g0 · ln(m0/m1) is displayed with the player's own numbers for every stage, together with liftoff thrust-to-weight ratio (must be ≥ 1.2), a Δv budget bar for each mission leg, and cost. A failed test explains where the propellant ran out, how many m/s were missing and what to try (add a second stage, use a vacuum engine on top, improve the mass ratio). Attempts can be compared side by side.

4.⁠ ⁠First-person flight. Launch is flown from an Orion-style cockpit with four camera views: cockpit, hull camera, orbit X-ray and external. The player triggers stage and fairing separation; whether the rocket reaches orbit is decided by the same Δv computed in the builder, so the outcome is honest and predictable.

5.⁠ ⁠3D orbit X-ray. In the DART mission the player flies on a 3D orbital map built on a two-body Kepler model (elliptic and hyperbolic orbits, Kepler's equation solved numerically). X-ray mode reveals velocity and gravity vectors, periapsis and apoapsis, the Hohmann transfer to the Moon, the direct-escape hyperbola and the Δv of each maneuver. Time warp goes up to 1,000,000×.

6.⁠ ⁠Random events and decisions. A randomized propellant leak can leave too little Δv for direct departure, forcing a choice between a lunar gravity assist and a direct escape. The other missions include anomalies based on real mission history (loss of Deep Space Network signal, hazardous landing terrain at Jezero, the OSIRIS-REx sample leak, the Psyche xenon line pressure drop), each with trade-offs in propellant and score.

7.⁠ ⁠Flight debrief. DART ends with a heliocentric transfer to Didymos, manual targeting of Dimorphos and a debrief table comparing the player's flight time, impact speed and orbital period change with the real NASA DART results. After a failure, the second attempt flies next to a "ghost" of the first one.

EDUCATIONAL IMPACT

Players learn why rockets have stages, why the logarithm in the rocket equation punishes dry mass, why vacuum engines differ from sea-level engines, what Δv budgets and thrust-to-weight mean, and how transfers and gravity assists work. Simplified values are labeled as educational estimates, and simulated telemetry is labeled as simulated.

TECHNOLOGY

JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js r187 (WebGL), Rapier 3D physics for character movement, Vite build, Web Audio API for procedural sound, CSS2D/SVG overlays for the cockpit and holographic panels, glTF/GLB models with Draco and meshopt compression, Blender Python scripts for scene building, Playwright for end-to-end tests and screenshots. Deployed as a static site on Vercel.

CREATIVITY AND ENGINEERING DECISIONS

•⁠ ⁠One shared physics core: the builder, the launch and the final outcome all use the same Δv calculation.

•⁠ ⁠A brute-force solver checks about 39,000 rocket configurations per mission to guarantee that every mission is solvable within its budget; it runs as part of the build.

•⁠ ⁠The cockpit is an SVG/CSS layer over the live 3D scene, so it adds depth without costing frame rate.

•⁠ ⁠Every external model has a procedural fallback, and the game runs offline except for the live asteroid radar.

•⁠ ⁠NASA 3D Resources models (SLS, Orion, DART, Perseverance, OSIRIS-REx) are normalized to real-world scale.

LIMITATIONS

Physics is deliberately simplified: two-body orbits, rounded Δv requirements and a compressed ascent timeline. The full orbital-map flight is implemented for DART; the other missions use a shorter cruise phase with one decision event.
